y-m-44-01.title: The spot that is the same distance from two harbors for a rescue boat
y-m-44-01.topic: The set of points that are the same distance from two points (the perpendicular bisector of a segment)
y-m-44-01.goal: Find points by hand to check that the points equally far from two points do not form just one point but a line, and explain with equations why they form a line.
y-m-44-01.material: There are two harbors at sea. On a coordinate plane (1 square = 1 km), harbor A is at (0, 0) and harbor B is at (6, 2). So that a rescue boat runs the same distance whichever harbor has an accident, you want to station it at a spot that is the same distance from both harbors.
y-m-44-01.thinking.0: Testing a predicted shape with points
y-m-44-01.thinking.2: Telling a few examples apart from a general reason
y-m-44-01.prereq.0: School-order assumption: the H1 of this task is only a difficulty level for this production batch and does not mean the curriculum fixes a grade. Assume the learner has already studied equations of figures (lines and circles) in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-44-01.prereq.1: Prior knowledge: how to find the distance between two points on a coordinate plane, and setting two expressions equal and expanding.
y-m-44-01.s.s1.prompt: Suppose you mark every point at sea that is the same distance from both harbors A and B. What shape do those points form together?
y-m-44-01.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one point other than (3, 1), the midpoint of segment AB, and write its distance to A and its distance to B. (Example: (2, 4))
y-m-44-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find three or four points, plot them on the coordinate plane, and look at which figure they line up on.
y-m-44-01.s.s1.o.a: Only the midpoint of segment AB, and no other point
y-m-44-01.s.s1.r.a: The midpoint is just one of the points at equal distance. Pick one more point and compare its distances to A and B.
y-m-44-01.s.s1.o.b: A circle with center A that passes through B
y-m-44-01.s.s1.r.b: A point on that circle is only the same distance from A. In this problem the distances to both A and B must be equal to each other.
y-m-44-01.s.s1.o.c: One line that passes through the midpoint of segment AB
y-m-44-01.s.s1.r.c: You can test this prediction by plotting a few points and checking what shape they line up in.
y-m-44-01.s.s1.o.d: A line through the two harbors A and B
y-m-44-01.s.s1.r.d: Points on line AB are often closer to one harbor. Compare the two distances using a few points on it.
y-m-44-01.s.s1.explain: Points at equal distance from A and B include not only the midpoint (3, 1) of segment AB but also far-away points such as (2, 4). These points lie on the line that passes through the midpoint of AB and meets AB at a right angle (the perpendicular bisector of segment AB). This is only a prediction for now; in the next step you will find points yourself to check.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.prompt: On the coordinate plane, right (east) is x and up (north) is y. The harbors are A(0, 0) and B(6, 2), and 1 square is 1 km. You want to station the rescue boat at a lattice point (a point where x and y are both integers). Conditions: you can use only sea where x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0, the point is the same distance from A and B, and it is within 10 km of A. Find and enter 3 different spots.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.hint.0: When you choose a point, write the square of the distance to A, x² + y², and the square of the distance to B separately, and compare the two values.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.hint.1: Fix x as 0, 1, 2, ... one at a time, then change y and look for where the two values become equal.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.ok.c1: It is in the sea (x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0).
y-m-44-01.s.s2.fail.c1: You can use only sea where x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.fail.c2: x and y must be integers.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.ok.c3: It is the same distance from A and B.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The distance to A and the distance to B are different. Compare their squares.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.ok.c4: It is within 10 km of A.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.fail.c4: It is farther than 10 km from A.
y-m-44-01.s.s2.explain: The lattice points that fit the conditions are four: (3, 1), (2, 4), (1, 7), (0, 10). They line up by the rule that y goes down by 3 each time x goes up by 1. (4, −2) is outside the sea, so it is left out.
y-m-44-01.s.s3.prompt: The points you found lie on one line. A few points that look like a straight line are not enough to say that all such points form a line. Write in your own words why the condition of equal distance becomes a line when written with x and y (or what reason you have to believe it is a line).
y-m-44-01.s.s3.hint.0: Take a point P(x, y) and write the equation that sets the square of the distance from P to A equal to the square of the distance from P to B.
y-m-44-01.s.s3.hint.1: Expand both sides and see whether any terms appear on both sides.
y-m-44-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Writing 'the distance to A equals the distance to B' as an equation gives ...
y-m-44-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation separate 'a few points look like a line' from 'the simplified equation is a line'?
y-m-44-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check what happens to terms like x² and y² in the equation?
y-m-44-01.s.s3.model.0: Point P(x, y) is the same distance from A and B, so PA² = PB², that is, x² + y² = (x−6)² + (y−2)². When you expand, the x² and y² on both sides cancel, leaving a first-degree expression in x and y such as 3x + y = 10, so it is a line.
y-m-44-01.s.s3.model.1: The four points you found lying in a row is only an example, not a proof. If you square the equal-distance condition and simplify, the x² and y² terms cancel on both sides and leave a first-degree equation, so you can say it is a line.
y-m-44-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that expresses the same idea in a different order.

y-m-44-02.title: Distance from a drone station to a road: where did the solution go wrong?
y-m-44-02.topic: The distance between a point and a line, and two parallel lines at the same distance
y-m-44-02.goal: Find the line where a solution for the distance between a point and a line goes wrong, check the result another way, and discover that points at the same distance lie on both sides of the road.
y-m-44-02.material: A drone station P is at (1, 5) on a coordinate plane (1 square = 1 km), and the equation of the straight road l is 3x + 4y − 30 = 0. A student posted a solution for 'the shortest distance from P to the road'.
y-m-44-02.thinking.1: Choosing an independent way to check
y-m-44-02.prereq.0: School-order assumption: the H1 of this task is only a difficulty level for this production batch and does not mean the curriculum fixes a grade. Assume the learner has already studied equations of figures (lines and circles) in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-44-02.prereq.1: Prior knowledge: assume the learner has learned once how to find the distance between a point and a line and knows the meaning of absolute value.
y-m-44-02.s.s1.prompt: Below is a solution for the shortest distance from the drone station P(1, 5) to the road l : 3x + 4y − 30 = 0. Choose the first line that goes wrong. (1 square = 1 km)
y-m-44-02.s.s1.hint.0: Check one by one how each line came from the line above it and where the numbers used come from.
y-m-44-02.s.s1.hint.1: Match the coefficients in the line equation 3x + 4y − 30 = 0 with the numbers in line 3.
y-m-44-02.s.s1.line.0: Find the distance between the point P(1, 5) and the line 3x + 4y − 30 = 0.
y-m-44-02.s.s1.line.1: Putting the point's coordinates into the left side of the line's equation gives 3·1 + 4·5 − 30 = −7.
y-m-44-02.s.s1.line.2: The denominator is made from the coefficients: √(3 + 4) = √7.
y-m-44-02.s.s1.line.4: So the distance from P to the line is √7 (about 2.65).
y-m-44-02.s.s1.explain: It goes wrong at line 3. The denominator squares the coefficient 3 of x and the coefficient 4 of y and adds them: √(3² + 4²) = 5. √(3 + 4) forgot to square. Then the distance is 7 ÷ 5 = 1.4 km. Lines 4 and 5 are wrong because they inherited the wrong value from line 3.
y-m-44-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to check whether the solution's result of √7 km is right by a different route, without repeating the same calculation. Choose all the methods that can be used to judge separately whether the result is right.
y-m-44-02.s.s2.hint.0: Decide whether each method is a 'different route' from the first solution or just repeats the same calculation.
y-m-44-02.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what property the 'shortest distance' must satisfy compared with any point on the road.
y-m-44-02.s.s2.o.a: Calculate once more in the same order as the first solution and compare whether the two values are equal
y-m-44-02.s.s2.r.a: Repeating the same order produces the same mistake again. You need a different route.
y-m-44-02.s.s2.o.b: Drop a perpendicular from P to the road, meeting it at a point H, and measure the distance PH directly
y-m-44-02.s.s2.r.b: A good check. The point on the road nearest to P is the foot of the perpendicular, so the distance to that point is exactly the value you want.
y-m-44-02.s.s2.o.c: Measure the distance from P to the point (10, 0), where the road meets the x-axis, and see whether it equals √7
y-m-44-02.s.s2.r.c: (10, 0) is just one point on the road, with no guarantee that it is the nearest point. It would not be strange for it to differ from the shortest distance.
y-m-44-02.s.s2.o.d: See whether the distance to one point on the road that looks close to P is shorter than √7
y-m-44-02.s.s2.r.d: No point on the road can be closer to P than the value you want. If a shorter one appears, it is evidence that the result is wrong.
y-m-44-02.s.s2.o.e: The answer came out as the irrational number √7, so the form of the value looks odd and the solution is judged wrong
y-m-44-02.s.s2.r.e: A distance can be irrational. You cannot tell right from wrong from the form of the value alone.
y-m-44-02.s.s2.explain: Method b directly shows that the distance to the foot of the perpendicular H(46/25, 153/25) is 1.4. Method d takes the point (2, 6) on the road, whose distance to P is √2 ≈ 1.41, shorter than √7 ≈ 2.65, which shows that '√7 is the shortest distance' is wrong. Both methods use a different route from the first solution, so they check the result independently.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.prompt: The correct distance is 7/5 km. Find and enter 3 different lattice points (x and y both integers) other than P(1, 5) that are at the same distance (7/5 km) from the road l. The range is 0 ≤ x ≤ 12, 0 ≤ y ≤ 10.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write what value 3x + 4y − 30 must have for the distance to be 7/5.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.hint.1: That value may not be only one. Write all the possible cases, and in each one choose x and fit y.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.fail.c1: It is outside the range 0 ≤ x ≤ 12, 0 ≤ y ≤ 10.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.fail.c2: x and y must be integers.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.ok.c3: The distance to the road l is 7/5 km.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.fail.c3: The absolute value of 3x + 4y − 30 is not 7. Check again whether the distance is 7/5.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.ok.c4: It is a point other than P.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.explain: The points that fit are (5, 2), (3, 7), (7, 4), (11, 1). They split into the points with 3x + 4y = 23 (on the same side as P) and the points with 3x + 4y = 37 (on the opposite side of the road).
y-m-44-02.s.s3.because.prompt: The points you found are not only on one side of the road but split into two branches. Explain why they are not on just one line.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.because.hint.0: Write again how the value of the expression that determines the distance relates to 7.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.because.hint.1: Imagine whether there are points at the same distance on one side of the road and on the opposite side.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: On both sides of the road ...
y-m-44-02.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include the two cases 'the value of the expression is 7 or −7'?
y-m-44-02.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you picture two sides at the same distance on either side of the road?
y-m-44-02.s.s3.because.model.0: For the distances to be equal, the absolute value of 3x + 4y − 30 must be 7. The value can be 7 or −7, so one parallel line forms on each side of the road.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.because.model.1: Points at the same distance from the road are on both the upper side and the lower side of the road. So two lines parallel to the road form and the points split into two branches.
y-m-44-02.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: An answer explained with a picture instead of equations.

y-m-44-03.title: Is a circle determined uniquely by this information alone?
y-m-44-03.topic: The information needed to determine the equation of a circle uniquely (sufficiency of information)
y-m-44-03.goal: Separate the information sets that determine exactly one circle from those that do not (several circles, or none), and fill in missing information on your own.
y-m-44-03.material: You want to make a problem in which a circle must be determined uniquely. Six groups received different information, and depending on the information, a circle may be determined uniquely, there may be several, or there may be none at all.
y-m-44-03.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-44-03.thinking.1: Showing with examples that several circles exist
y-m-44-03.prereq.0: School-order assumption: the H1 of this task is only a difficulty level for this production batch and does not mean the curriculum fixes a grade. Assume the learner has already studied equations of figures (lines and circles) in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-44-03.prereq.1: Prior knowledge: the meaning of the equation of a circle (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r², and the distance between two points.
y-m-44-03.s.s1.prompt: Six groups received the information below. Choose all the groups for which the information alone determines exactly one circle that fits the conditions. (The circles are on a coordinate plane; units are omitted.)
y-m-44-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, check whether the 'center' and the 'radius' are each determined.
y-m-44-03.s.s1.hint.1: For groups that are not determined, split them into 'several circles' or 'no circle'. Test by moving the position of the center once.
y-m-44-03.s.s1.o.a: (가) The center is (3, −1) and it passes through the point (6, 3)
y-m-44-03.s.s1.r.a: If you have the center and a point it passes through, the distance between them is the radius, so the circle is determined uniquely.
y-m-44-03.s.s1.o.b: (나) The center is on the line y = x and the radius is 5
y-m-44-03.s.s1.r.b: The center can be anywhere on the line. If you change the position of the center a few ways, you can check whether the circle is determined uniquely.
y-m-44-03.s.s1.o.c: (다) It passes through the three points (0, 0), (2, 0), (4, 0)
y-m-44-03.s.s1.r.c: The three points are on one line. Think about whether there is a circle that passes through all three.
y-m-44-03.s.s1.o.d: (라) The two ends of a diameter are (1, 2) and (7, 10)
y-m-44-03.s.s1.r.d: If you know the two ends of a diameter, both the center (the middle point) and the radius are determined.
y-m-44-03.s.s1.o.e: (마) It passes through the two points (0, 0), (6, 0) and the radius is 5
y-m-44-03.s.s1.r.e: Check whether a circle with radius 5 passing through the two points has only one possible center. The center must be the same distance from the two points.
y-m-44-03.s.s1.o.f: (바) It passes through the three points (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 2)
y-m-44-03.s.s1.r.f: If three points are not on one line, there is exactly one circle through them.
y-m-44-03.s.s1.explain: (가) is determined with radius 5, (라) with center (4, 6) and radius 5, and (바) with center (2, 1) and radius √5. (나) has infinitely many, as many as the center can move along the line; (다) has no circle through them because the three points are on one line; and (마) has two, since the center can be (3, 4) or (3, −4).
y-m-44-03.s.s2.prompt: Check directly that in (마) there are several circles, not one. Enter 2 different centers (a, b) of circles that pass through the two points (0, 0), (6, 0) and have radius 5.
y-m-44-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write two equations that make the square of the distance from the center to (0, 0) and the square of the distance to (6, 0) each equal to 25.
y-m-44-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the two equations to find the value that a is determined to be, then look at all the values b can take.
y-m-44-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The distance from (0, 0) to the center is 5.
y-m-44-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The distance from (0, 0) to the center is not 5.
y-m-44-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The distance from (6, 0) to the center is 5.
y-m-44-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The distance from (6, 0) to the center is not 5.
y-m-44-03.s.s2.explain: The centers are the two points (3, 4) and (3, −4). A center at the same distance from the two points must be on x = 3, and on that line there are two places, one above and one below, where the radius is 5.
y-m-44-03.s.s3.prompt: For (나) and (다), write why each does not determine a circle uniquely, and write how you could change or add just one piece of information in each to make the circle determined uniquely.
y-m-44-03.s.s3.hint.0: For (나), move the center along the line and think about how many circles of radius 5 you get.
y-m-44-03.s.s3.hint.1: For (다), roughly plot the three points on the coordinate plane and imagine whether you can draw a circle through all of them.
y-m-44-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: (나) is ... so ... if we also tell ...
y-m-44-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain (나) and (다) separately? Did you avoid lumping them under one reason?
y-m-44-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check directly that the information you added really determines the circle uniquely?
y-m-44-03.s.s3.model.0: In (나) the center can be anywhere on the line y = x, so there are infinitely many circles of radius 5. If you tell the x-coordinate of the center, it is determined uniquely. In (다) the three points are on one line, so no circle passes through them. If you move the third point off the line, it is determined uniquely.
y-m-44-03.s.s3.model.1: In (나) the position of the center is not fixed, so there are several circles; it would help to know one more point the circle passes through. In (다) the three points are on one line, so a circle cannot be drawn; one point must be changed to somewhere off the line.
y-m-44-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: Another answer that uses both adding and changing.

y-m-44-04.title: The moment the triangle made by three lines disappears
y-m-44-04.topic: The positions of three lines (meeting at one point, parallel) and the conditions for making a triangle
y-m-44-04.goal: Review the cases where three lines cannot form a triangle (parallel, meeting at one point) in the order the information is revealed, and summarize the conclusion for each value of k.
y-m-44-04.material: There are three lines l₁ : y = x + 1, l₂ : y = −x + 5, l₃ : 2x − y = k. k is a constant. Depending on the value of k, the three lines may or may not enclose a triangle. How to read: l₃ is 'two x minus y equals k'.
y-m-44-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the conditions are enough
y-m-44-04.thinking.1: Revising a judgment with new information
y-m-44-04.thinking.2: Finding the special case and explaining why
y-m-44-04.prereq.0: School-order assumption: the H1 of this task is only a difficulty level for this production batch and does not mean the curriculum fixes a grade. Assume the learner has already studied equations of figures (lines and circles) in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-44-04.prereq.1: Prior knowledge: finding the intersection of two lines, and finding the area of a triangle from the coordinates of its three vertices (using base and height or using coordinates).
y-m-44-04.s.s1.prompt: Information about the three lines is revealed one piece at a time at each step. Each time, choose the reasonable thought given the information so far.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write which part of the 'conditions for a triangle to form' the newly revealed information changes.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether it is fine to keep the same choice or whether you have to change the reason.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.0.info: There are three lines. l₁ : y = x + 1 (slope 1), l₂ : y = −x + 5 (slope −1), l₃ : 2x − y = k (slope 2, k is a constant not yet fixed). The slopes of the three lines are all different, so no two of them are parallel.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Whatever number k is, the three lines are not parallel to each other. Then, whatever k is, do the three lines make a triangle?
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Having no parallel lines is only one of the conditions for a triangle to form. There may be, depending on k, another way that a triangle does not form (the three lines meeting at one point), so you need to check.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The three lines are not parallel to each other, so a triangle forms whatever k is
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Did you think about the case where the three lines meet at one point? Even if they are not parallel, a triangle may not form.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Depending on k a triangle may not form, so we need to check more
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You pointed out that 'not parallel' alone does not settle the conclusion. What remains is finding out which cases are the problem.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: They are not parallel, so a triangle never forms
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: If there are three different intersection points, those three points become the vertices of a triangle.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.1.info: The intersection of l₁ and l₂ is (2, 3). Putting (2, 3) into the equation 2x − y = k of l₃ gives 4 − 3 = 1.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: When k = 1, do the three lines make a triangle?
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If k = 1, l₃ also passes through (2, 3), so all three intersection points overlap into the single point (2, 3). Only one point is left instead of a triangle, so no triangle forms.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The intersection (2, 3) is on all three lines, so there are three intersection points and a triangle forms
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: A triangle forms only when the three intersection points are three different points. What happens if the intersections of the three lines merge into one?
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The three lines all become the same line, so no triangle forms
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The slopes of the three lines are different: 1, −1, 2, so they can never be the same line.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The three lines meet at the one point (2, 3), so no triangle forms
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You pointed out that they meet at one point, so the three intersection points overlap into one.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.2.info: This time let k = 3. The intersection of l₁ and l₃ is (4, 5), the intersection of l₂ and l₃ is (8/3, 7/3), and the intersection of l₁ and l₂ is (2, 3). These three points are the vertices of the triangle.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: When k = 3, what is the area of the triangle enclosed by the three lines?
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.2.after: Using the three vertices (2, 3), (4, 5), (8/3, 7/3), the area is 4/3. Finding the intersection of two lines, checking whether they meet at one point, and finding the area of a triangle are all connected.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This value is twice some value. Check whether you forgot the step of halving when finding the area of a triangle.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Put in the coordinates of the three vertices and calculate again. You may have picked the base and height wrongly.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You found the area from the coordinates of the three vertices.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This looks like the product of the coordinate differences as it is. A triangle is half of a rectangle.
y-m-44-04.s.s1.reflect: At first it is easy to think 'if they are not parallel, a triangle will form'. How did your judgment change at each step? At which step did your 'confidence' grow as information increased, and at which step did the 'conditions' increase?
y-m-44-04.s.s2.prompt: Find all the cases (how many are there?) in which the three lines cannot make a triangle depending on the value of k, and write the reason in one or two sentences.
y-m-44-04.s.s2.hint.0: First find the intersection of l₁ and l₂, then find the k that makes l₃ pass through that point.
y-m-44-04.s.s2.hint.1: Pick one other value of k and check whether the three intersection points become different from each other.
y-m-44-04.s.s2.placeholder: Example: A triangle does not form only when k is ... Because ...
y-m-44-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether the k you found is the 'only' value, and why other values of k do not work?
y-m-44-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you include in your reason the fact that there is no parallel case?
y-m-44-04.s.s2.model.0: It does not form only when k = 1. Then the three lines all pass through the one point (2, 3), so the three intersection points overlap into one. The slopes are all different, so there is no parallel case.
y-m-44-04.s.s2.model.1: The only case is when l₃ passes through the intersection (2, 3) of l₁ and l₂, that is, when k is 1. Then the three lines meet at one point and make no triangle. For any other k, the intersections are three different points.
y-m-44-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that also gives the reason for 'only'.

y-m-44-05.title: Two friends' ways to find a symmetric point: which one is right?
y-m-44-05.topic: Reflection of a point across a line
y-m-44-05.goal: Compare two ways of finding a symmetric point, sort out the conditions under which each method works, and make pairs of points that are symmetric.
y-m-44-05.material: This is a problem of finding the point Q that you get by reflecting the point P(4, 1) across the line m : y = x + 1. Units are omitted.
y-m-44-05.thinking.1: Stating the conditions where it holds
y-m-44-05.thinking.2: Making many examples within a condition
y-m-44-05.prereq.0: School-order assumption: the H1 of this task is only a difficulty level for this production batch and does not mean the curriculum fixes a grade. Assume the learner has already studied equations of figures (lines and circles) in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-44-05.prereq.1: Prior knowledge: finding the midpoint of two points, the condition for two lines to be perpendicular (slopes), and the meaning of reflecting a point.
y-m-44-05.s.s1.prompt:
You need to find the point Q obtained by reflecting the point P(4, 1) across the line m : y = x + 1. You compared two friends' methods.
하늘 : "Reflecting across y = x means swapping the x-coordinate and y-coordinate. So Q is (1, 4)."
다온 : "Choose Q so that PQ meets m at a right angle and the midpoint of PQ is on m."
Which judgment about the two methods fits best?
y-m-44-05.s.s1.hint.0: Find the midpoint of 하늘's point Q(1, 4) and P(4, 1), and put it into the equation of the line m.
y-m-44-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write 다온's two conditions (perpendicular, midpoint) as equations, find a and b for Q(a, b), and compare with 하늘's point.
y-m-44-05.s.s1.o.a: 하늘's method can be used whatever shape the line has, so Q(1, 4) is right
y-m-44-05.s.s1.r.a: Test whether the method of swapping the x- and y-coordinates also works for this line by checking whether the midpoint of P and Q(1, 4) is on m.
y-m-44-05.s.s1.o.b: Both methods can be used, and the points they give are the same
y-m-44-05.s.s1.r.b: Calculate directly to compare whether the two methods give the same point. You can tell by checking whether the point from one side satisfies the conditions.
y-m-44-05.s.s1.o.c: When the line is not y = x, there is no way to determine the reflected point
y-m-44-05.s.s1.r.c: Even when the line is not y = x, there are conditions that determine the point. Look at which of the two friends' methods uses the conditions.
y-m-44-05.s.s1.o.d: 다온's method should be used, and 하늘's method works only when the line is y = x
y-m-44-05.s.s1.r.d: You sorted out the methods on the basis of the meaning of reflection (perpendicular and midpoint). You also pointed out when 하늘's method works.
y-m-44-05.s.s1.explain: The reflected point Q satisfies 'PQ is perpendicular to the line' and 'the midpoint of PQ is on the line'. Solving with 다온's conditions gives Q(0, 5). 하늘's Q(1, 4) has midpoint (2.5, 2.5), and this point is not on y = x + 1, so it is wrong. 하늘's method is right only when the line is y = x.
y-m-44-05.s.s2.prompt: Make pairs of points that are symmetric across the line m : y = x + 1. Call the point with the smaller x-coordinate (p, q) and the one with the larger x-coordinate (r, s), and all are integers from 0 to 10. Enter 3 different pairs.
y-m-44-05.s.s2.hint.0: Choose the coordinates (p, q) of one point, and find an expression that writes the coordinates of the symmetric point using p and q. First pick one pair yourself and check the midpoint and slope.
y-m-44-05.s.s2.hint.1: Test whether the rule you found also works for other pairs by checking whether the midpoint is on m.
y-m-44-05.s.s2.var.p: x-coordinate p of the left point
y-m-44-05.s.s2.var.q: y-coordinate q of the left point
y-m-44-05.s.s2.var.r: x-coordinate r of the right point
y-m-44-05.s.s2.var.s: y-coordinate s of the right point
y-m-44-05.s.s2.fail.c1: All four numbers must be from 0 to 10.
y-m-44-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Write the point with the smaller x-coordinate as (p, q).
y-m-44-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The two points are symmetric across the line m.
y-m-44-05.s.s2.fail.c3: Fit the coordinates so that the midpoint of the two points is on m and the line joining them is perpendicular to m.
y-m-44-05.s.s2.explain: Symmetric points are (p, q) and (q − 1, p + 1). For example, for (0, 5) and (4, 1), the midpoint (2, 3) is on m, and the slope of the line joining the two points is −1, so it is perpendicular to m. This is the expression you get by swapping x and y as 하늘 did and then correcting by 1.
y-m-44-05.s.s3.prompt: Write for which kind of line 하늘's method (swapping the x-coordinate and y-coordinate) is right, and explain, using P(4, 1) and Q(1, 4), why it is not right for the line m in this problem.
y-m-44-05.s.s3.hint.0: Find the coordinates of the midpoint of P and Q(1, 4) and check whether that point satisfies the equation of the line m.
y-m-44-05.s.s3.hint.1: Change the line to y = x, apply the same method, and compare what changes.
y-m-44-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: 하늘's method is right only when the line is ... In this problem Q(1, 4) is ..., so ...
y-m-44-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write both 'when' 하늘's method works and 'why' it does not work in this problem?
y-m-44-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check with numbers the evidence you used (such as the midpoint)?
y-m-44-05.s.s3.model.0: 하늘's method is right only when the line is y = x. The midpoint of P(4, 1) and Q(1, 4) is (2.5, 2.5), but the line m : y = x + 1 has only points where y is 1 greater than x, so this point is not on m. So they are not symmetric.
y-m-44-05.s.s3.model.1: Swapping x and y gives the point symmetric across y = x. m is the line y = x moved up by 1, so you need to move once more. The distances from P and Q(1, 4) to m are not equal, so 하늘's point is wrong.

y-m-44-06.title: A booth next to the fountain: is a spot on the boundary allowed?
y-m-44-06.topic: Points inside a region determined by a circle and a line (regions of inequalities, whether the boundary is included)
y-m-44-06.goal: In a region given by inequalities for a circle and a line, read separately for each condition whether the boundary is included, make several points that satisfy the conditions, and explain the effect of changing a condition.
y-m-44-06.material: A park map is shown on a coordinate plane (1 square = 10 m). The fountain is at (2, 1), and the places where a booth can be set up are the lattice points that satisfy all three conditions below. ㈎ The distance from the fountain is at most 4 (boundary included), that is, (x − 2)² + (y − 1)² ≤ 16. ㈏ Above the line y = x − 5, that is, y > x − 5 (a spot on the line is a walkway, so a booth cannot be set up). ㈐ x ≥ 0.
y-m-44-06.thinking.0: Checking the conditions one by one separately
y-m-44-06.thinking.2: Predicting the effect of changing a condition
y-m-44-06.prereq.0: School-order assumption: the H1 of this task is only a difficulty level for this production batch and does not mean the curriculum fixes a grade. Assume the learner has already studied equations of figures (lines and circles) in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-44-06.prereq.1: Prior knowledge: the regions shown by inequalities for a circle and a line (inside/outside, above/below).
y-m-44-06.s.s1.prompt: A student wants to decide whether a booth can be set up at the point (6, 1). Choose the most fitting judgment.
y-m-44-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write ㈎, ㈏, ㈐ one at a time and make a table of ○ and × showing whether (6, 1) satisfies each.
y-m-44-06.s.s1.hint.1: Find which condition has the point on its boundary, and check in the wording of the problem whether that condition includes the boundary.
y-m-44-06.s.s1.o.a: It can be set up: the distance from the fountain is exactly 4 (the boundary of the circle), and the boundary is included, so it is allowed
y-m-44-06.s.s1.r.a: You checked only the circle condition. You must also check the line condition ㈏.
y-m-44-06.s.s1.o.b: It cannot be set up: it satisfies ㈎, but it is a point on the line y = x − 5, so it fails ㈏
y-m-44-06.s.s1.r.b: You checked the three conditions separately and judged that failing even one means no. You read that whether the boundary is included differs from condition to condition.
y-m-44-06.s.s1.o.c: It cannot be set up: the distance from the fountain is 4, so it does not fall under 'at most 4'
y-m-44-06.s.s1.r.c: 'At most' includes 4 as well. Read the wording of the condition again.
y-m-44-06.s.s1.o.d: Cannot tell: the problem does not say whether points on the boundary are included
y-m-44-06.s.s1.r.d: The problem states for each condition whether the boundary is included. Read the text of the conditions again.
y-m-44-06.s.s1.explain: (6, 1) is at distance 4 from the fountain (2, 1), so it satisfies ㈎ (boundary included). But substituting into y = x − 5 gives 1 = 6 − 5, so it is a point on the line and falls under ㈏'s 'a spot on the line is excluded'. The boundary is treated differently in each condition, so you have to check them separately.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.prompt: Make candidate booth sites by entering 4 different lattice points (x and y integers) that satisfy all of the conditions ㈎, ㈏, ㈐.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.hint.0: Fix one x first and find the range of y that satisfies ㈎.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.hint.1: From that range, cross out the y that do not satisfy ㈏ and choose from the y that remain.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must be integers.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.ok.c2: ㈎ The distance from the fountain is at most 4.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.fail.c2: It does not satisfy ㈎. Check whether the square of the distance from the fountain (2, 1) is at most 16.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.ok.c3: ㈏ It is above the line y = x − 5.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.fail.c3: It does not satisfy ㈏. A point on the line is not allowed; it must be above the line.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.fail.c4: It does not satisfy ㈐. x must be at least 0.
y-m-44-06.s.s2.explain: There are 36 lattice points in all that fit the conditions. Many answers are possible, such as (2, 1), (3, 2), (0, 1), (2, 4). (6, 1) is left out because it is on the line, (6, 3) because its distance from the fountain is √20 > 4, and (−1, 1) because x < 0.
y-m-44-06.s.s3.prompt: Suppose that later condition ㈎ is changed from 'at most 4' to 'less than 4' (boundary excluded). Check whether any of the points you just entered change; if so, explain which points and why, and if not, explain why not.
y-m-44-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write the square of the distance from the fountain for each point you wrote and compare it with 16.
y-m-44-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how the result differs between 'at most' and 'less than' when the value is exactly 16.
y-m-44-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Among my points, ... is at distance ... from the fountain, so ...
y-m-44-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether any of your points is at a distance of exactly 4 from the fountain?
y-m-44-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: When there is none, did you also write 'why there is none'?
y-m-44-06.s.s3.model.0: My point (2, 5) is at distance exactly 4 from the fountain (2, 1), so it drops out if changed to 'less than 4'. The other points have distance less than 4, so they stay as they are.
y-m-44-06.s.s3.model.1: My points are (2, 1), (3, 2), (0, 1), (2, 4), and all of them are at distance less than 4 from the fountain, so they stay the same even if changed to 'less than'. The only points that change are the boundary points at distance exactly 4.
y-m-44-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: Another answer explaining that there is no effect because there are no boundary points.

y-m-44-07.title: Testing the claim 'if the vertices have integer coordinates, the area is an integer too'
y-m-44-07.topic: The area of a triangle given by coordinates and integer coordinates (testing a claim with a counterexample)
y-m-44-07.goal: Understand that a single example cannot settle an 'always' claim, make a counterexample, and fix the claim so it is true.
y-m-44-07.material: Your friend 지수 said, "The area of a triangle whose vertices all have integer coordinates is always an integer!" Units are omitted. Hint: the area of triangle OAB with vertices at the origin O(0, 0), A(p, q), B(r, s) is |ps − qr| ÷ 2.
y-m-44-07.thinking.0: Testing with examples whether a generalization is true
y-m-44-07.thinking.2: Fixing the claim by stating its conditions
y-m-44-07.prereq.0: School-order assumption: the H1 of this task is only a difficulty level for this production batch and does not mean the curriculum fixes a grade. Assume the learner has already studied equations of figures (lines and circles) in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-44-07.prereq.1: Prior knowledge: even and odd integers and absolute value, and how to find the area of a triangle from coordinates (in this task the formula is used as a given fact).
y-m-44-07.s.s1.prompt: 지수 said, "The area of a triangle whose vertices all have integer coordinates is always an integer!" 지수 checked by making triangle OAB with O(0, 0), A(4, 0), B(0, 3), and the area was 6. How should you judge 지수's statement from this one example?
y-m-44-07.s.s1.hint.0: Instead of O, A, B, pick two or three other sets of integer-coordinate vertices and find the areas.
y-m-44-07.s.s1.hint.1: Change the vertices to very small numbers, like (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1).
y-m-44-07.s.s1.o.a: One example cannot settle it, so look further for an example that does not fit
y-m-44-07.s.s1.r.a: A claim of 'always' is broken by a single wrong example, no matter how many right examples there are. Looking for a wrong example tests the claim more strongly.
y-m-44-07.s.s1.o.b: If one or two more right examples come up, then consider the claim settled
y-m-44-07.s.s1.r.b: Even with two or three right examples, you have not checked 'every case'.
y-m-44-07.s.s1.o.c: 6 is an integer, so settle that 지수's claim is right from this example
y-m-44-07.s.s1.o.d: There is the condition of integer coordinates, so the statement is true without even looking for examples
y-m-44-07.s.s1.r.d: Having a condition does not mean the statement holds in every case under that condition. You need to test a few cases.
y-m-44-07.s.s1.explain: A statement 'always holds' cannot be settled by collecting examples that fit, and it is broken by one example that does not fit (a counterexample). So looking for an example that does not fit is the most direct way to test the claim.
y-m-44-07.s.s2.prompt: The area of triangle OAB made of the origin O(0, 0), A(p, q), B(r, s) is |ps − qr| ÷ 2. (Reading: the absolute value of p times s minus q times r, divided by 2) Make and enter 3 triangles whose vertices all have integer coordinates (from −9 to 9) but whose area is not an integer, with 3 different areas.
y-m-44-07.s.s2.hint.0: First pick a few p, q, r, s that make |ps − qr| odd. You can start from the smallest case, where the value is 1.
y-m-44-07.s.s2.hint.1: After making one example, change just one number so that |ps − qr| becomes a different odd number.
y-m-44-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The absolute values of all four numbers must be at most 9.
y-m-44-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The coordinates must all be integers.
y-m-44-07.s.s2.ok.c3: |ps − qr| is odd, so the area is not an integer.
y-m-44-07.s.s2.fail.c3: Is the area not an integer? Check whether |ps − qr| is odd.
y-m-44-07.s.s2.explain: For example, for O(0, 0), A(1, 0), B(0, 1), |1·1 − 0·0| ÷ 2 = 1/2; for A(2, 1), B(1, 2) it is 3/2; and for A(3, 1), B(1, 2) it is 5/2. All have integer coordinates but the area is not an integer, so 지수's statement does not hold.
y-m-44-07.s.s3.prompt: Fix 지수's statement so that it is true. Write what kind of number |ps − qr| must be for the area of an integer-coordinate triangle to be an integer, and what form of number the area will be.
y-m-44-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write |ps − qr| and the area side by side for the three examples you made, and look for a pattern.
y-m-44-07.s.s3.hint.1: Make one example where |ps − qr| is even and compare whether the area is an integer.
y-m-44-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The area is an integer only when |ps − qr| is ... So if we fix it to '...', it is true.
y-m-44-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In your sentence, is it clear which values (even/odd) correspond to 'when it is an integer' and 'when it is not an integer'?
y-m-44-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check that your fixed sentence fits all three examples you made?
y-m-44-07.s.s3.model.0: The area is an integer only when |ps − qr| is even. If it is odd, the area is (odd) ÷ 2, so a .5 is attached. So if we fix it to 'the area is an integer or an integer plus 0.5', it is true.
y-m-44-07.s.s3.model.1: The area of an integer-coordinate triangle has the form (integer) ÷ 2. If |ps − qr| is even, it is an integer, and if it is odd, it is not an integer and a half (0.5) is left. Fixing it this way also explains the counterexamples 1/2, 3/2, 5/2.
y-m-44-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: Another answer stated in the form (integer) ÷ 2.

y-m-44-08.title: A line comes back to where it was, so why can't a circle?
y-m-44-08.topic: Cases in which a translation maps a line or a circle onto itself
y-m-44-08.goal: Compare the equations of translated figures to find the condition under which a line maps onto itself (n = 2m), and explain why a circle has no such translation.
y-m-44-08.material: If you translate a figure on the coordinate plane m to the right and n up, every point of the figure moves in the same direction by the same distance. Let's move the line y = 2x + 1 and the circle (x − 1)² + (y + 2)² = 9 and look at the results.
y-m-44-08.thinking.0: Revising a judgment with experiment results
y-m-44-08.thinking.1: Making many translations that satisfy a condition
y-m-44-08.thinking.2: Explaining the difference between a line and a circle
y-m-44-08.prereq.0: School-order assumption: the H1 of this task is only a difficulty level for this production batch and does not mean the curriculum fixes a grade. Assume the learner has already studied equations of figures (lines and circles) in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-44-08.prereq.1: Prior knowledge: how the equation changes under translation (replace x with x − m and y with y − n), the slope of a line, and the center and radius of a circle.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.prompt: The results of translation experiments are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose the reasonable thought given the information so far.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the result of the translation at each step directly with the original equation and write whether they are the same or different.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the new information changes your judgment. If it does not, write the reason in one line.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.0.info: When the line y = 2x + 1 was moved 3 to the right and 1 up, it became y = 2x − 4. (It is a different line from before the move.)
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: Is it possible to move this line onto itself by a translation?
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.0.after: Just because one move gave a different line, you cannot say every translation does. There is a reason to test other moves.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A translation always makes a line a different line, so it is impossible to move it onto itself
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You said 'always' from one test. Test again with a different direction of movement.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Depending on the direction and distance of the move, it might become the same line
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You pointed out that you should not be tied to one result and should test other moves too.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: This one result alone doesn't tell us; we need to try other moves too
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is the judgment of putting off the conclusion and doing another test. It is reasonable.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.1.info: When moved 1 to the right and 2 up, y − 2 = 2(x − 1) + 1, that is, y = 2x + 1, so it became the same as the original line.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: Then if you move it 2 to the right and 4 up, will it also be the same line?
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.1.after: When moved by (2, 4), y − 4 = 2(x − 2) + 1, that is, y = 2x + 1, the same line again. This is because the direction of the move (1, 2) is parallel to the slope 2 of the line.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: If the distance moved is different, the result is different too, so it will be a different line
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even if the distance is different, a move in the direction parallel to the line can give the same line. Compare the direction of the move with the slope of the line.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is the same line only for 1 to the right and 2 up, and no other move works
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: (2, 4), twice the move (1, 2), has the same direction. Put it in and check directly.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It seems it will be the same line. Put it in and check directly
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is the judgment of predicting the result and testing it directly.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.info: Moving m to the right and n up gives y = 2x − 2m + n + 1. For this to be the same as the original line y = 2x + 1, n = 2m is needed. Now suppose we move the circle (x − 1)² + (y + 2)² = 9 m to the right and n up.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which translations (m, n) map the circle onto itself?
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.after: The center of the circle moves from (1, −2) to (1 + m, −2 + n). For the circle to be the same, the center must be the same, so only (m, n) = (0, 0). A line is still the same line when it slides by a move in its own direction, but a circle has no such direction.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: A move with n = 2m makes the circle map onto itself, just as with the line, so it is the same circle
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Check what happens to the center of the circle. Unlike a line, a circle has no 'track' parallel to the direction of movement.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Only (0, 0). Any other move changes the center and gives a different circle
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You judged by the center and radius of the circle. Even with the same radius, a different center means a different circle.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The radius is the same, so any translation gives the same circle
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The radius is the same but the position changes. Check where the center of the circle goes.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.o.d: A circle is round, so no matter which direction or how far you push it, it stays itself
y-m-44-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Being round does not mean it maps onto itself. Compare the coordinates of the center.
y-m-44-08.s.s1.reflect: At first it is easy to think 'a translation turns a line into a different line'. How did your thinking change according to the experiment results? Why is the 'move that maps onto itself' different for a line and a circle?
y-m-44-08.s.s2.prompt: Among the translations (m to the right, n up) that map the line y = 2x + 1 onto itself, make and enter 3 different ones, leaving out the case of no movement (m = 0). m and n are integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-44-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write the moved equation in the form y = 2x + (something) and find the condition that makes its y-intercept equal to that of the original line.
y-m-44-08.s.s2.hint.1: Once you find one pair, also test a move that has the same direction but a different distance.

y-m-44-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you point out the differences between a line and a circle (a line has a direction, a circle has a center)?
y-m-44-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Does your reason connect to where the center coordinates (1, −2) of the circle go?
y-m-44-08.s.s2.because.model.0: The center of the circle moves from (1, −2) to (1 + m, −2 + n). If (m, n) is not (0, 0), the center changes and it becomes a different circle, so there is nothing other than (0, 0). A line has a direction to slide along, but a circle does not.
y-m-44-08.s.s2.because.model.1: A line overlaps itself when moved in a direction parallel to itself, but a circle's center moves when pushed in any direction, so it does not overlap. Only when the center is the same (when it does not move) is it the same circle.
y-m-44-08.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: An answer written from the viewpoint of 'direction'.
